Scan an otpauth:// QR code, paste an otpauth:// link, or add manually (name, issuer, secret, algorithm, digits, period).\n\nGoogle Authenticator users can migrate via Settings → Data → Google Authenticator quick import.

Codes refresh every 30 seconds (or your custom period). Tap a code to copy it. The progress bar shows the remaining time.\n\nThe clock is essential: if codes keep failing, check your device clock and adjust it under Settings → Security → Clock calibration.
Settings → Appearance → Sort mode: manual (add order), alphabetical, add time, or copy count. Accounts can no longer be reordered by dragging.

Steam accounts must be added MANUALLY: issuer = Steam, secret = the Base32 shared secret. The app then generates the 5-character alphanumeric Steam codes automatically.\n\nQR codes and otpauth:// links for Steam are intentionally not imported — Steam Guard has no official TOTP standard, and manual entry keeps the special format explicit.

HOTP codes do not refresh by themselves. Tap \u201CNext code\u201D in the account details to advance the counter (+1). The counter persists per account. Use HOTP only when the service explicitly requires it.

• Require verification on open: fingerprint / system password / Osmium PIN before showing codes.
• Self-destruct PIN: entering it at ANY PIN prompt wipes all accounts after a confirmation.
• Screenshots are blocked by default; you can allow them in Settings, but hidden data stays protected.
• Osmium never connects to anything except the WebDAV backup server you configure yourself and the GitHub releases API for update checks (when auto-check is enabled) — no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud.
Settings → Data → Export creates an encrypted backup (password + app PIN). Keep the password safe — without it the backup cannot be restored. Google Authenticator migration is read-only import.

Settings → Data → WebDAV backup uploads the same encrypted export file to a WebDAV server on your local network — a NAS, a PC, or another phone running a WebDAV server app. Fill in the server address (hostname or LAN IP), username and password.

Restore lists the backups stored on the server and lets you pick one to restore. Manage backups lists the same backups and can delete old ones from the server. The server only ever receives password-encrypted data; the app never connects to anything except the server address you configure.

If the server address keeps changing, give the NAS a fixed IP in your router settings, or use its hostname.

Open https://otp.osmium.im to verify that Osmium (or any authenticator) generates correct codes: the site issues a test secret, you add it to your app and enter the code back. It supports TOTP, HOTP and Steam Guard with multiple algorithms, digit counts and periods — fully in-browser, nothing is uploaded.

Both the account name and the issuer are optional.

If you leave the ACCOUNT NAME blank, Osmium generates one automatically from the add date and the add order — e.g. the first account added in May 2026 is named 20260501.

If you leave the ISSUER blank, it is shown as "Unknown".

• Secrets are encrypted with a non-exportable Android Keystore key; they leave the device only inside your own password-encrypted backups.
• Uninstalling the app or clearing its data DELETES all accounts — export a backup first.
• Copied codes stay in the clipboard; there is no auto-clear.
• If your device clock is wrong, codes will be wrong — enable network time sync.

By installing or using Osmium, you agree to the following terms.

Osmium is free and open source software released under the MIT License (LICENSE in the repository).

The software is provided "as is", without warranty of any kind. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the developer is not liable for any damages arising from the use of the software.

Your responsibilities:
• Safeguard your secrets and backup passwords. Encryption keys cannot be recovered by the developer or anyone else — a forgotten PIN or lost backup password cannot be reset. The automatic-backup password is stored on your device (encrypted with the Android Keystore) and is unrecoverable if the app's data is erased.
• Keep backups. Uninstalling the app or clearing its data permanently deletes all accounts. Automatic backups run unattended via the Android system scheduler and depend on the device's power state and background-activity settings (see the README); the app keeps no persistent background service and does not drain the battery beyond the short backup job.
• The self-destruct PIN is irreversible, by design.
• Keep your device clock accurate — time-based codes depend on it.

You may use Osmium for your own two-factor authentication. You may not use it to access systems or data you are not authorized to access.

Osmium runs no account system and connects to no third-party services except the WebDAV server you configure yourself (backups are encrypted with your password before upload) and the GitHub releases API for the optional update check, which sends no account or device data. The Google Authenticator migration feature parses export codes locally on the device.

Osmium does not collect any data. There is no account system, no registration, no analytics, no advertising SDK, and no crash reporter.

Storage: your secrets, account names and issuers are stored only on this device, encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a non-exportable key in the Android Keystore. Backup files are encrypted with your password (PBKDF2 + AES-256-GCM). The WebDAV server address and login are stored on your device, with the password encrypted by the Android Keystore.

Network: the INTERNET permission is used for two optional features only. (1) WebDAV backup: the app connects only to the server address you configure — typically a NAS or PC on your local network — and only when you run a backup or restore. Plaintext http:// addresses require an explicit on-screen confirmation. (2) Update checks: when auto-check is enabled, the app asks the GitHub releases API for the latest public version every time the app opens; no account or device data is sent.

Automatic backup: scheduled backups run unattended via the Android system scheduler. The export password you set is stored encrypted with the Android Keystore key and is used only to encrypt backup files. Local backups are written to the public Download/Osmium folder; a configurable number are kept (default 5, max 10) and older ones are pruned. The app keeps no persistent background service and does not drain the battery beyond the short backup job.

Camera: used only to scan QR codes, processed on-device; frames are never stored or transmitted.

Biometrics: handled exclusively by the Android system; the app never sees or stores fingerprint or face data.

Storage permission (Android 8/9 only): WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE is requested only on Android 8 and 9, solely to write automatic backups to the public Download/Osmium folder.

We share nothing, because we hold nothing. Uninstalling the app deletes all locally stored data.

Any future change affecting these guarantees will be stated in the release notes.

Settings → Data → Auto backup runs an unattended backup on a schedule: pick a target (WebDAV server or phone storage), an interval in days, and a time of day. The next run time is shown with a GMT+8 label.

Backups use the same password-encrypted export format as manual backups. The export password is stored encrypted with the Android Keystore key and is used only to encrypt backup files. Local backups are written to the public Download/Osmium folder; a configurable number of auto-backups are kept (default 5, max 10) and older ones are pruned.

The last run result is shown on the auto-backup screen. A backup that fails (e.g. no server reachable) is recorded there and retried once; the next scheduled run tries again.

When auto-check is enabled (Settings → About → Auto-check for updates), Osmium silently asks the GitHub releases API for the newest version every time the app opens. If a newer version exists, a dialog offers to open the GitHub releases page — it never downloads or installs anything by itself.\n\nNo account data or device information is sent; the request only asks for the latest public release. The check stays silent on network failures.
Older backups are deleted beyond this count (max 10)
